newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Philharmonic names Ashkenazy chief conductor.
newsitem.headline: Czech Philharmonic names Ashkenazy chief conductor.

text.p: Russian-born maestro Vladimir Ashkenazy was appointed chief conductor of the Czech Philharmonic on Wednesday, saying he wanted the orchestra to be recognised among the world's best.

Ashkenazy told a news conference his contract, beginning next January for an initial three-and-a-half-year period, would include conducting concerts in Prague and abroad, recording and developing the orchestra.
"If we make good music, if the orchestra is recognised as one of the great orchestras in the world, if we present versatile programmes...that's all I'm after," he said.
Ashkenazy will spend up to eight weeks a year in Prague and conduct up to eight concerts a season. But he also said he wanted to be involved in the orchestra's day-to-day work.

"Any suggestions, questions or discussions about the work of the orchestra, where it is going, what they would like to do, I would like to be part of it otherwise what is the point of being the chief conductor. I don't want just a title."

The Czech Philharmonic was hit by scandal at the beginning of last year when German Gerd Albrecht quit as chief conductor after a long dispute with the orchestra's management which took on nationalist overtones.
Asked about the row, Ashkenazy, who is also a world-renowned pianist, said his aim was to make good music and have the Czech Philharmonic recognised as one of the world's great orchestras.
"I'm a born musician, I have to make good music. That is all I can do, I do my best and the rest is in God's hands," he said

Jiri Kovar, the orchestra's general director, described Ashkenazy as a long-time friend of the country. The Soviet-led Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 to crush the Prague Spring contributed to Ashkenazy's decision to renounce his Soviet citizenship.
